argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Modus tollens and reductio ad absurdum
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: Moderate - some premises are implicit, especially about the nature of time and God's knowledge as an event

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: High - engages with multiple objections and alternative views
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: High - all arguments directly address the compatibility of foreknowledge and freedom
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Moderate - relies on controversial assumptions about time and God's nature

distinctions_drawn: Changing the past vs. bringing about the past
explicit_definitions_given: Libertarian freedom: ability to do otherwise
Soft determinism: freedom as acting on desires

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Systematic - addresses circularity, memory, and time intuitions

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Philosophical arguments, thought experiments, appeals to physics

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Analytic philosophy with focus on logical and ontological analysis
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Divine foreknowledge, human freedom, time, and modality

structural_organization.structure_type: Problem-solution with dialectical progression through objections

summary_of_core_decisions: The paper argues that divine foreknowledge and libertarian freedom are logically compatible by defending the possibility of changing God's past beliefs in a non-causal sense. It rejects soft determinism, addresses objections about circularity, memory, and time, and appeals to a B-theory of time to undermine intuitions about the inalterability of the past.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low - states conclusion confidently but acknowledges need for further work on providence
